title: Optimize CPU request path: reduce serialization and thread contention, add thread pinning
author: Arjun Patel
description:
Motivation: CPU-side request path is a measurable bottleneck for small, high-concurrency requests. We see tail latency dominated by request serialization/deserialization, mutex contention in the global thread pool, and OS-level scheduling jitter. This PR reduces per-request CPU overhead by minimizing copies during serialization, introducing a fast-path for hot request types, splitting the request worker pool into dedicated shards, and adding optional CPU pinning for workers on dedicated nodes.

What changed (summary): 1) Zero-copy request buffer: replace a couple of intermediate std::string copies with a Span-backed serializer and move-only message objects to avoid memcpy. 2) Fast-path parsing: pre-parse common headers and cache parsed proto slices for warmup request types; requests that match the fast-path skip the general deserializer. 3) Thread pool sharding: replace the single global request thread pool with a shard-aware pool (N shards per CPU socket) to reduce lock contention and improve cache locality. 4) Optional CPU pinning: new runtime flag runtime.cpu_request_pinning and per-node config to pin worker threads to a contiguous CPU set using sched_setaffinity on Linux; fallback to original behavior if pinning fails. 5) Lock contention reduction: use a single-producer single-consumer ring for per-shard queues and change a few hot mutexes to atomic state transitions. 6) Telemetry and canary: added new metrics (cpu.request.fast_path_hits, cpu.request.queue_wait_ms by shard) and a perf canary that runs the microbenchmark suite on canary nodes.

Performance: microbench on m5-like CPU + small request payloads: 95th percentile latency reduced from 14.6ms to 10.5ms (~28% reduction). End-to-end throughput on a CPU-bound workload increased ~18% when running 5000 rps synthetic load. P99 reduction is more modest (~12%) but consistent across runs. Memory and heap usage unchanged.

Safety and rollout: change is behind a runtime feature flag (runtime.cpu_request_fast_path) and node-level pinning toggled via node config. Default is disabled for pinned mode in hosted. We will rollout via canary: enable fast_path on 5% of serving nodes -> monitor cpu.request.fast_path_hits, request.latency.* and error rates -> increase to 25% -> 100%. Pinning is an opt-in for Dedicated/private customers and enabled for internal perf nodes.

Testing: unit tests for serializer and ring buffer, integration test exercising both fast and slow paths, added perf-canary job that compares baseline and optimized branch. Bench results are captured in benchmark artifacts and linked in the CI output.

Notes: this PR intentionally keeps ABI stable; no proto changes. We validated on x86_64 Linux; pinning is a no-op on macOS and Windows in our test harness. See release_notes for rollout summary.

review_comments: Sofia Martinez: Can you share the perf runs across different payload sizes? Looks great for small requests but we should verify mid-sized (1-2KB) do not regress.
Author (Arjun): Added additional bench runs to perf-canary artifacts and included 1KB/2KB series; no regressions observed, numbers pushed to CI artifacts.
Lena Wang: Thread pinning looks fine but please add fallback and a clear error path if sched_setaffinity fails; also document behavior on multi-socket machines.
Author (Arjun): Added fallback logic to leave threads unpinned on error and documented socket-aware shard count in docs/runtime_flags.md.
Marcus O'Neill: Suggest changing the default shard count heuristic; using sockets rather than logical cores prevents cross-socket cache bounce. Made that change during review.
Sofia Martinez (approve): Verified perf-canary graphs and unit tests, LGTM after minor doc tweaks.
ci_checks: perf-canary: initial run failed on first iteration due to missing bench artifact, rerun passed
release_notes: Reduced CPU request path latency by ~28% P95 and increased throughput ~18% for CPU-bound small-request workloads. Feature gated behind runtime.cpu_request_fast_path and node-level pinning opt-in. Backwards compatible; no proto changes.
additional_context: This PR addresses a long-standing CPU bottleneck called out in ENG-1982. The change is primarily performance-focused; behavioral surface remains unchanged. Observability hooks and canary plan included. We will monitor rollout metrics closely and have an automatic rollback plan if errors or latency regressions exceed thresholds.
